hints: Start by thinking about what must be put into the virus - where would you get a working copy of the eye gene if the patient does not have one?
Recall the standard genetic engineering toolkit for cutting and joining DNA once you have isolated the wanted gene.
Think about how to make enough copies of the gene to work with, and how to make sure it will be switched on in human retina cells.
Link the enzymes to their jobs - one creates sticky ends, the other seals the backbone to form recombinant viral DNA.
walkthrough:
Get the Working Allele**
You need a normal, functional version of the gene that is faulty in LCA. This can be synthesised as cDNA made from mRNA isolated from cells of a healthy person, or taken from a gene library and identified using a DNA probe, sequencing or electrophoresis.

Amplify and Prepare It**
Use PCR to amplify the therapeutic DNA so there is enough to use. To allow expression in the retina, a promoter sequence must be added upstream of the gene.

Cut and Paste into the Vector**
Cut both the therapeutic DNA and the AAV vector DNA with the same restriction endonuclease to produce complementary sticky ends. Then seal the sugar-phosphate backbones together with DNA ligase to create recombinant DNA containing the therapeutic allele.

Final answer: Obtain normal / therapeutic dominant allele as cDNA from mRNA of healthy person / gene library, identified by probe / sequencing / electrophoresis; amplify by PCR; cut allele and AAV DNA with same restriction endonuclease and join with DNA ligase; add promoter.

hints: Think about what recessive means for the patient's cells - what proteins are they missing?
Compare adding a gene with removing a gene - why is adding one working copy enough here?
walkthrough:
One Working Copy Is Enough**
In autosomal recessive LCA both alleles are faulty, so no functional protein is made. Adding just one normal dominant allele per cell is enough for transcription and translation of the correct functional protein.

No Need to Remove the Faulty Alleles**
Because the faulty alleles are recessive, they do not block the action of the added allele. Gene therapy can simply add the therapeutic DNA to cure the disease and restore vision, without having to knock out or delete the faulty alleles.
Final answer: Only one normal / dominant allele per cell needs to be added to synthesise functional protein and restore vision / correct phenotype; no need to remove / edit faulty recessive alleles.

hints: Compare the starting vision of the two groups - LCA patients blind from birth versus older people who can still see but are slowly losing vision.
Think about the worst outcome of the injection - retinal detachment - and who has less to lose if it goes wrong.
walkthrough:
Weigh the Risk of Detachment**
Direct injection into the retina can cause the retina to detach and damage vision further. That is a serious risk.

Why LCA Patients First**
LCA patients are already blind from birth, so there is little remaining vision to lose. It is ethically safer to trial a risky delivery method first in people who cannot be made much worse, before using it in older patients who still have useful vision to protect.

Final answer: LCA patients are already blind / have lost vision from a young age, so retinal injection causing detachment is less likely to harm / worsen vision compared with patients who still have vision.

hints: Focus on the stage of PCR where new DNA is actually built onto the template strand.
Remember the properties of the heat-stable enzyme used in PCR compared with normal human DNA polymerase.
Think about what happens to a single mistake when PCR keeps cycling over and over.
walkthrough:
Mistake During Extension**
In the extension stage of PCR, DNA polymerase builds a new strand complementary to the template strand. Occasionally the wrong base pairs with the template, creating a base-pair mismatch - a base substitution.

Why Taq Makes More Mistakes**
PCR uses Taq polymerase because it is heat-stable, but it is inaccurate and has no 3-prime to 5-prime proofreading ability to remove wrong bases, so errors remain.

Errors Are Amplified**
That mutant strand then acts as template in the next cycles, so the mistake is copied many times and spreads through the population of AAV DNA molecules.

Final answer: During extension / elongation Taq polymerase with no proofreading adds wrong base / creates base-pair mismatch to template DNA; error is then replicated / copied many times in later cycles.

hints: Trace the journey of the virus in step 3 - from injection site to the target cells.
Remember what GFP does when its gene is switched on inside a cell - why use it as a test gene?
walkthrough:
Delivery to the Retina**
The recombinant virus carrying the GFP gene was able to cross the fluid inside the eye and reach the photoreceptor cells in the retina, then deliver its DNA into those cells.

Expression Gives Fluorescence**
Inside the photoreceptors the GFP gene was transcribed and translated. The GFP protein product is fluorescent, so successfully infected cells glow brightly, proving delivery and expression worked.
Final answer: 7m8 / vector crossed fluid and reached photoreceptors / retina and delivered GFP gene / DNA; gene expressed to produce fluorescent GFP / protein product, so cells fluoresce.

hints: Think about what step 3 proved - injection into fluid worked as well as injection into retina - and what risk that avoids.
walkthrough:
Safer Treatment**
Because 7m8 can reach photoreceptors from the fluid inside the eye, there is no need for direct retinal injection. This decreases the risk of retinal detachment and makes treatment for age-related retinal diseases safer and more effective.
Final answer: 7m8 allows injection into eye fluid instead of retina, decreasing risk of retinal detachment and improving gene therapy treatment.
